newsitem.title: USA: Former top aide sees lingering woes for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Former top aide sees lingering woes for Clinton.

text.p: The mushrooming campaign fund-raising controversy may become a lingering problem for President Bill Clinton, a former top aide said on Wednesday amid new calls for a probe by a special prosecutor.

One day after the White House released documents showing that the president had enthusiastically encouraged inviting big money donors to stay overnight at the White House, even those closest to him admitted that the issue may fester.

"This is going to be a lot of trouble over this year for the president," George Stephanopoulos, Clinton's former senior adviser whose White House office was near the president's Oval Office, told ABC's Good Morning America programme.
Stephanopoulos left the administration in January to teach at New York's Columbia University and to work as a political commentator for ABC.
"If the line was crossed, people will be punished," he said. "But this paper doesn't show that the line was crossed. It does show that people were going right up to the edge."

The paper in question is a stack of documents, released by the White House on Tuesday, that provide a detailed look at White House involvement in the Democratic Party's frenzied effort to raise money before the 1996 presidential election.

Buried in the stack of paper was a handwritten note from Clinton endorsing a memo from then Democratic fund-raising chief Terry McAuliffe that proposed inviting the party's top 20 supporters to breakfast, lunch or coffee with Clinton.
The memo proposed setting dates for such get-togethers with the president for major backers, listed the top 10 contributors, and proposed including supporters in golfing or jogging outings.
An attached note in Clinton's handwriting said: "Yes pursue all 3 (goals) and promptly -- and get other names at 100,000 or more 50,000 or more."
The handwritten note added: "Ready to start overnights right away."

Clinton on Tuesday denied he used the overnight stays to induce wealthy backers to make big donations, saying: "They were my friends and I was proud to have them here...I did not have any strangers here. The Lincoln Bedroom was never sold."

The release of the documents, which were held by Clinton's former deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes, prompted a series of calls for an independent counsel to investigate the matter, including one on Tuesday by Republican Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott.
Others made similar calls on Wednesday.
"I think there will probably be independent counsel but it's long overdue and way late," Republican Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania said in an interview on CNN.
